palette.notes: Frames: purple and blue-grey stone floors, dark red rugs; bright accents for bullets (white/red rings), gold items and a cyan guide arrow. Enemy bullets are the most saturated thing on screen.

lighting: Dim dungeon rooms lit by small light sources (torches, a muzzle flash, a white bloom at a door); bright effects glow on dark floors.
silhouette: Tiny heroes with hats and big guns; enemies are living bullets (Gundead, wiki) with a cartridge body and a face. Bosses are big round shapes with a mouth (clip 3, 42 s).

motion.timing: No frame timings measured. Bullet patterns form shapes (rings, heart faces) and expand outward slowly enough to read (clip 2). Dodge roll gives brief invulnerability (wiki).

texture: Crisp tiles with brick lines, framed portraits and crates as props; shell casings litter the floor after fights.
camera: Top-down, follows the player in the room; item pickups get a big framed card that pops over the scene (clip 3, 6-14 s).

acting.enters: Enemies come as a crowd; in the Gungeon 2 trailer (3D, not pixel) a pile of hundreds of bullet characters becomes one tower.
acting.acts: Bullet characters are props with faces: the joke is the object being alive. Bosses fire bullet patterns that form faces and hearts.
acting.exits: Enemies burst into shell casings that stay on the floor.
acting.depth: One plane; scale gag from many tiny copies vs one big boss.

techniques: object as character: a bullet with eyes and feet
bullet patterns that draw shapes (rings, smiley faces, hearts)
crowd of identical tiny characters as a gag
item card pop-over to name a pickup
feel: dark purple rooms + bright bullet patterns + tiny living-bullet enemies = playful chaos you can read
for_fred: Turn a prop into a character the Gungeon way: give a small object eyes and a 2-frame waddle, then multiply it (one, then ten copies) behind Fred for a scale gag. Avoid giving every prop a face; one living prop per reel.
